title: Nearly 100 Grameen Bank branches attacked this month, says Yunus
excerpt: In a statement, Muhammad Yunus said branches were petrol-bombed almost daily in November and that 97% of the bank's 11 million borrowers are women.

image.alt: A woman in rural Bangladesh feeds a cow she bought with a microfinance loan
image.credit: File photo: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (Australia) / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0

content:
Grameen Bank branches have been attacked with petrol bombs almost every day since the start of November, and nearly 100 branches have been hit this month, former chief adviser Professor Muhammad Yunus said in a statement on Monday (23 November), Prothom Alo reported.

Yunus said attackers chanted "Joy Bangla" during the incidents and that the pattern led him to believe they were acting on instructions. Devlens has not been able to verify the number of attacks independently, and police have not published a count.

He said 97% of Grameen Bank's 11 million borrowers are women, that the loan recovery rate is above 95%, and that borrowers own 90% of the bank's shares, with the government holding the rest. He said he has had no role in the bank's ownership or management since he was removed as managing director in 2011.

According to the statement, bank staff and borrowers narrowly escaped serious harm in several attacks, and Grameen Bank has asked the home ministry for more security for its borrowers, staff and records. Yunus thanked law enforcement for steps already taken and called for those responsible to be brought to justice quickly. Devlens reported an arson attack on a Grameen Bank office in Muksudpur, Gopalganj, on 19 November.

Why it matters

Grameen Bank is one of the country's largest microfinance lenders. Attacks on branches put staff and borrowers at risk and can interrupt loan collection, savings and new lending for poor rural women. Other microfinance institutions and NGOs with field offices will be watching security in the same areas.

What to watch

Whether police publish figures and make arrests, whether the home ministry provides the security the bank requested, and whether attacks spread to other microfinance or NGO offices.

Sources
